rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun and moon provide immense benefits, as several other Qur’anic passages also state.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن الانتفاع بالشمس والقمر عظيم ، وقد ذكره الله تعالى في آيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dāʾibayn means proceeding continually in a regular course of activity.
rows.anchor: معنى الدؤب في اللغة مرور الشيء في العمل على عادة مطردة

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The sun and moon continually move, illuminate, remove darkness, and affect the flourishing of plants and animals.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون : قوله : { دائبين } معناه يدأبان في سيرهما وإنارتهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun governs daytime and the moon nighttime; without the sun there would be no four seasons and worldly interests would collapse.
rows.anchor: فإن الشمس سلطان النهار والقمر سلطان الليل ولولا الشمس لما حصلت الفصول الأربعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an also describes night as covering people and day as the time for livelihood, and night as rest and day as illumination.
rows.anchor: كقوله تعالى : { وجعلنا اليل لباسا * وجعلنا النهار معاشا } ( النبأ : 10 ، 11 )

rows.speaker: المتكلمون
rows.claim: Calling night and day subjugated is metaphorical, since they are accidents and accidents cannot be subjugated.
rows.anchor: قال المتكلمون : تسخير الليل والنهار مجاز لأنهما عرضان ، والأعراض لا تسخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted object in “He gave you of all you asked” is estimated as a portion of every requested thing; God gave far more benefits than can be counted.
rows.anchor: والمفعول محذوف تقديره من كل مسؤول شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading gives kullin tanwīn and treats mā as negation in a circumstantial accusative: God gave from everything without their asking.
rows.anchor: وقرىء : { من كل } بالتنوين و { ما سألتموه } نفي ومحله نصب على الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, mā is relative: God supplied everything people needed for sound life and livelihood, as though they had asked by their state.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تكون ( ما ) موصولة والتقدير : آتاكم من كل ذلك ما احتجتم إليه

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Niʿma is a noun used in place of the verbal noun inʿām, so it is not pluralized because it carries a collective verbal sense.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي : النعمة ههنا اسم أقيم مقام المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You cannot enumerate them” means people cannot count all God’s blessings because of their abundance.
rows.anchor: أي لا تقدرون على تعديد جميعها لكثرتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Studying the nerves shows why blessings cannot be enumerated: cranial and spinal nerves branch into countless delicate pathways, each with a specific function whose disruption harms the body.
rows.anchor: أن الأعصاب قسمان ، منها دماغية ومنها نخاعية . أما الدماغية فإنها سبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each tiny nerve branch is a great blessing, and humans cannot inspect its condition or enumerate its benefit; the same applies to arteries, veins, and every organ.
rows.anchor: عرف أن الله تعالى بحسب كل شظية من تلك الشظايا العصبية على العبد نعمة عظيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same inexhaustible complexity extends from the body to the soul, animals, celestial spheres, elements, land, sea, plants, and creatures.
rows.anchor: فاعرف أقسام نعم الله تعالى في نفسه وروحه ، فإن عجائب عالم الأرواح أكثر من عجائب عالم الأجساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even all created intellects combined could discern only a little of divine wisdom in the smallest things.
rows.anchor: أن عقول جميع الخلائق لو ركبت وجعلت عقلا واحدا ثم بذلك العقل يتأمل الإنسان في عجائب حكمة الله تعالى في أقل الأشياء لما أدرك منها إلا القليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Understanding even one bite of bread requires the whole world’s order: wheat depends on seasons, elements, weather, and celestial motions, while its tools depend on iron and prior tools.
rows.anchor: لأن الحنطة لا بد منها ، وأنها لا تنبت إلا معونة الفصول الأربعة ، وتركيب الطبائع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Understanding what follows a bite requires anatomy and medicine, since one must know how the body uses food and where eating can harm it.
rows.anchor: فتأمل في تركيب بدن الحيوان ، وهو أنه تعالى كيف خلق الأبدان حتى يمكنها الانتفاع بتلك اللقمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These dependencies prove that even one blessing cannot be fully understood, confirming that blessings cannot be enumerated.
rows.anchor: فظهر بهذا البرهان القاهر صحة قوله تعالى : { وإن تعدوا نعمة الله لا تحصوها }

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The human is unjust by neglecting gratitude for blessings and intensely ungrateful by denying them.
rows.anchor: قيل : يظلم النعمة بإغفال شكرها كفار شديد الكفران لها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation says people complain and despair in hardship, then hoard and withhold during prosperity; “the human” denotes the species’ customary behavior.
rows.anchor: وقيل : ظلوم في الشدة يشكو ويجزع ، كفار في النعمة يجمع ويمنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because people forget or tire of blessings, they neglect gratitude; if they reflect on some blessings, they overlook others.
rows.anchor: فإذا وجد نعمة نسيها في الحال وظلمها بترك شكرها ، وإن لم ينسها فإنه في الحال يملها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast with 16:18 presents humans as unjust and ungrateful in receiving blessings, while God is forgiving and merciful in giving them.
rows.anchor: فأنت الذي أخذتها وأنا الذي أعطيتها ، فحصل لك عند أخذها وصفان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s forgiveness and mercy mean that human failure is answered with further provision and harshness with faithful generosity.
rows.anchor: إن كنت ظلوما فأنا غفور ، وإن كنت كفارا فأنا رحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children are transient adornments, so it is irrational to boast, rejoice, or assign them lasting worth; this rebuts wealthy polytheists’ taunts against poor believers.
rows.anchor: فهذا برهان باهر على فساد قول أولئك المشركين الذين افتخروا على فقراء المؤمنين بكثرة الأموال والأولاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lasting afterlife goods are better than perishing worldly goods; intellectual and spiritual goods outrank sensory ones, especially because the afterlife unites both kinds of happiness.
rows.anchor: وخيرات الآخرة دائمة باقية والدائم الباقي خير من المنقرض المنقضي

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: One view identifies the lasting good works as the four glorifications: Subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, and Allāhu akbar.
rows.anchor: قيل إنها قولنا : ( سبحان الله والحمد لله ولا إله إلا الله والله أكبر )

rows.speaker: الشيخ الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazali explains the fourfold reward as ascending knowledge: declaring God free of defect, recognizing Him as source of good, affirming His oneness, and acknowledging that His greatness exceeds reason’s grasp.
rows.anchor: وللشيخ الغزالي رحمه الله في تفسير هذه الكلمات وجه لطيف

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: A second reported interpretation identifies the lasting good works as the five daily prayers.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : أن الباقيات الصالحات هي الصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: A third interpretation takes them as good speech, as in the description of the people of Paradise.
rows.anchor: والقول الثالث : أنها الطيب من القول كما قال تعالى : { وهدوا إلى الطيب من القول }

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: A fourth view includes every deed or utterance that directs a person to know, love, and serve God; attention to all else is futile because it perishes.
rows.anchor: أن كل عمل وقول دعاك إلى الاشتغال بمعرفة الله وبمحبته وخدمته فهو الباقيات الصالحات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anything done for God yields better reward and hope, since its doer hopes for God’s reward in this life and a share in the next.
rows.anchor: أي كل عمل أريد به وجه الله فلا شك أن ما يتعلق به من الثواب وما يتعلق به من الأمل يكون خيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Meeting God can mean seeing Him: although liqāʾ originally means arrival or encounter, its familiar metaphorical use for seeing is preferable to inserting an unstated phrase meaning meeting His reward.
rows.anchor: حمل اللفظ على المجاز المتعارف المشهور أولى من حمله على ما يحتاج معه إلى الإضمار

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila infer from deeds being nullified that the doctrines of abatement and expiation are true; al-Razi refers the detailed discussion to al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: استدلت المعتزلة بقوله تعالى : { فحبطت أعمالهم } على أن القول بالإحباط والتكفير حق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation of having no weight is that God will disdain them and they will have no worth.
rows.anchor: الأول : أنا نزدري بهم وليس لهم عندنا وزن ومقدار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that no scales are set for them: scales distinguish good and bad deeds among monotheists.
rows.anchor: لا نقيم لهم ميزانا لأن الميزان إنما يوضع لأهل الحسنات والسيئات من الموحدين

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The Qadi says that when sins outweigh a person’s good deeds, the obedience counts as though it never existed, so none of it enters the weighing; this relies on abatement.
rows.anchor: الثالث : قال القاضي : إن من غلبت معاصيه صار ما في فعله من الطاعة كأن لم يكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That” refers to the punishments just detailed, and “Hell” is an appositional clarification of their punishment.
rows.anchor: ذلك الذي ذكرناه وفصلناه من أنواع الوعيد هو جزاؤهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their punishment answers both their disbelief and their additional mockery of God’s signs and messengers.
rows.anchor: لم يقتصروا على الرد عليهم وتكذيبهم حتى استهزأوا بهم

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators relate that Moses asked Shuʿayb to return to his mother, left with his family, had a child on a freezing snowy Friday night, lost the road, and saw a distant fire after his tinder would not catch.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون : استأذن موسى عليه السلام شعيبا في الرجوع إلى والدته فأذن له فخرج فولد له ابن

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Moses thought the distant light was a shepherd’s fire.
rows.anchor: قال السدي : ظن أنها نار من نيران الرعاة

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others say Moses saw the fire in a tree, though al-Razi says the Qur’anic wording does not establish that.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون : إنه عليه السلام رآها في شجرة وليس في لفظ القرآن ما يدل على ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the view that Moses merely imagined a fire, al-Razi holds that it was real, so Moses’ report was truthful; lying is impermissible for prophets.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنه رأى نارا ليكون صادقا في خبره إذ الكذب لا يجوز على الأنبياء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One classification says worldly fire eats without drinking, green-wood fire drinks without eating, stomach fire does both, and Moses’ fire does neither.
rows.anchor: نار تأكل ولا تشرب وهي نار الدنيا ، ونار تشرب ولا تأكل وهي نار الشجر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A second classification distinguishes fire with light but no burning (Moses’), burning without light (Hell), both (worldly), and neither (trees).
rows.anchor: نار لها نور بلا حرقة وهي نار موسى عليه السلام . وثانيها : حرقة بلا نور وهي نار جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “His family” may mean his wife, child, and servant together, or only his wife; the plural may reflect the ordinary collective meaning of family or respectful address to one person.
rows.anchor: فيجوز أن يكون الخطاب للمرأة وولدها والخادم الذي معها ويجوز أن يكون للمرأة وحدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ānastu means seeing distinctly and without doubt; the associated meanings explain why the word suggests visible humans, in contrast with hidden jinn.
rows.anchor: والإيناس الإبصار البين الذي لا شبهة فيه ومنه إنسان العين فإنه يبين به الشيء والإنس لظهورهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses says “perhaps” because obtaining a firebrand or guidance was still uncertain; this caution shows that he did not promise what he could not guarantee, contrary to the claim that Abraham lied for a good purpose.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الإيناس بالقبس ووجود الهدى مترقبين متوقعين بني الأمر فيهما على الرجاء والطمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A qabas is fire carried on the end of a stick, wick, or similar object; guidance is a source of direction or a sign to follow.
rows.anchor: والقبس النار المقتبسة في رأس عود أو فتيلة أو غيرهما : { أو أجد على النار هدى }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being “upon” the fire means being on nearby elevated ground or overlooking it, as people gathered around it are above it.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الاستعلاء على النار أن أهل النار يستعلون المكان القريب منها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas describes a green tree glowing white from bottom to top like fire, with neither the flame changing its greenness nor the tree’s moisture dimming the flame; Moses saw great light and heard angels glorifying God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رأى شجرة خضراء من أسفلها إلى أعلاها كأنها نار بيضاء

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb narrates that Moses approached the apparent fire with dry sticks; it moved toward him, retreated, repeatedly tempted him, then vanished, while the branch glowed skyward and a dazzling light appeared.
rows.anchor: قال وهب : فظن موسى عليه السلام أنها نار أوقدت فأخذ من دقاق الحطب ليقتبس من لهبها

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The Qadi allows that Moses’ tinder might fail, but says fire retreating before his prophethood is impossible unless it was a miracle for another prophet.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي الذي يروى من أن الزند ما كان يورى فهذا جائز وأما الذين يروى من أن النار كانت تتأخر عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi rejects the Qadi’s objection because the revelation that God chose Moses indicates this was the beginning of his prophethood, and pre-prophethood signs (irhāṣ) are possible.
rows.anchor: القاضي إنما بنى هذا الاعتراض على مذهبه في أن الإرهاص غير جائز وذلك عندنا باطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The immediate-sequence particle faʾ does not exclude a brief interval between Moses’ arrival and the call.
rows.anchor: تخلل الزمان القليل فيما بين المجيء والنداء لا يقدح في فاء التعقيب

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu ʿAmr reads the initial hamza of an-nī with fatḥ, making the call say, “I am your Lord.”
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو وابن كثير ( أنى ) بالفتح أي نودي بأني أنا ربك

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir shares the fatḥ reading; the other readers use kasr, either as direct address “Moses” or because a call is treated as speech.
rows.anchor: والباقون بالكسر أي نودي فقيل : يا موسى أو لأن النداء ضرب من القول

rows.speaker: الأشعري
rows.claim: Al-Ashʿari says God made Moses hear the pre-eternal divine speech, which is neither letters nor sound.
rows.anchor: قال الأشعري إن الله تعالى أسمعه الكلام القديم الذي ليس بحرف ولا صوت

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila deny pre-eternal speech and say God created the call in a body such as the tree, since He can create speech whenever He wills.
rows.anchor: وأما المعتزلة فإنهم أنكروا وجود ذلك الكلام فقالوا : إنه سبحانه خلق ذلك النداء في جسم من الأجسام

rows.speaker: أهل السنة من أهل ما وراء النهر
rows.claim: Transoxanian Sunnis affirm pre-eternal speech but say the sound Moses heard was created in the tree; the call follows his arrival at the fire, so the heard sound was temporal.
rows.anchor: وأما أهل السنة من أهل ما وراء النهر فقد أثبتوا الكلام القديم إلا أنهم زعموا أن الذي سمعه موسى عليه السلام صوت خلقه الله تعالى في الشجرة

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Al-Razi’s theological school says God may have given Moses immediate knowledge of the caller’s identity or made him recognize it through a miracle.
rows.anchor: فقال أصحابنا : يجوز أن يخلق الله تعالى له علما ضروريا بذلك ويجوز أن يعرفه بالمعجزة

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila reject immediate knowledge because it would entail necessary knowledge of the Creator and remove Moses from moral responsibility; they therefore require recognition through a miracle.
rows.anchor: قالت المعتزلة : أما العلم الضروري فغير جائز لأنه لو حصل العلم الضروري بكون هذا النداء كلام الله تعالى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One view says it is certain that God identified Himself through a miracle, without needing to specify which miracle.
rows.anchor: منهم من قال نعلم قطعا أن الله تعالى عرفه ذلك بواسطة المعجز ولا حاجة بنا إلى أن نعرف ذلك المعجز ما هو

rows.speaker: راوٍ
rows.claim: A report says Moses, after seeing the tree’s light and hearing angelic glorification, asked where the unseen speaker was; a doubt from Satan prompted him to infer that the voice was not created because he heard it from every direction.
rows.anchor: فقال : لبيك إني أسمع صوتك ولا أراك فأين أنت ؟

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another possibility is that Moses heard the call from an inanimate object such as pebbles, which would itself be a miracle.
rows.anchor: وثالثها : لعله سمع النداء من جماد كالحصى وغيرها فيكون ذلك معجزا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A further view says the fire in the green tree neither extinguished the greenery nor harmed it; only God could produce this sign.
rows.anchor: ورابعها : أنه رأى النار في الشجرة الخضراء بحيث أن تلك الخضرة ما كانت تطفىء تلك النار

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima interprets Ṭuwā as the name of the valley.
rows.anchor: الأول : أنه اسم للوادي وهو قول عكرمة وابن زيد

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd likewise interprets Ṭuwā as the name of the valley.
rows.anchor: وهو قول عكرمة وابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation derives Ṭuwā from “twice”: the valley was sanctified twice, or Moses was called twice.
rows.anchor: الثاني : معناه مرتين نحو مثنى أي قدس الوادي مرتين أو نودي موسى عليه السلام نداءين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says Moses crossed the valley at night; on this interpretation Ṭuwā is a verbal noun meaning he traversed it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما إنه مر بذلك الوادي ليلا فطواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One connection to the preceding account of a destroyed town is that cosmic creation shows the destruction was just retribution, not caprice; creation serves religious reflection and worldly benefit.
rows.anchor: لما بين إهلاك أهل القرية لأجل تكذيبهم اتبعه بما يدل على أنه فعل ذلك عدلا منه ومجازاة على ما فعلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second connection is proof of Muhammad’s prophethood: if he were false, God’s manifestation of a miracle for him would be play, which is impossible.
rows.anchor: أن الغرض منه تقرير نبوة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم والرد على منكريه

rows.speaker: القاضي عبد الجبار
rows.claim: Qadi ʿAbd al-Jabbar infers that play cannot come from God, because denying the agent-name “player” would entail denying the act of play.
rows.anchor: المسألة الثانية : قال القاضي عبد الجبار : دلت الآية على أن اللعب ليس من قبله تعالى إذ لو كان كذلك لكان لاعبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi rejects the Qadi’s inference by referring to the earlier argument from motive.
rows.anchor: والجواب : يبطل ذلك بمسألة الداعي عن ما مر غيره مرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From Us” may mean from God’s power; alternatively, lahw means a child in Yemeni usage or a wife, and “from Us” may mean angels rather than humans, rebutting claims that Jesus or Ezra is God’s son.
rows.anchor: معناه من جهة قدرتنا . وقيل : اللهو الولد بلغة اليمن وقيل : المرأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Rather” turns away from taking amusement or play: divine wisdom defeats play with seriousness and falsehood with truth, depicted as a hard projectile battering a soft body.
rows.anchor: تصويرا لإبطاله فجعله كأنه جرم صلب كالصخرة مثلا قذف به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat of woe addresses those who reject the Messenger and call the Qur’an magic, confused dreams, and other falsehoods.
rows.anchor: من تمسك بتكذيب الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم ونسب القرآن إلى أنه سحر وأضغاث أحلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A skeptic asks whether the destruction of earlier peoples might have resulted from planetary conjunctions rather than their disbelief, which would undermine the moral lesson of those stories.
rows.anchor: السؤال الأول : لم لا يجوز أن يقال : إن العذاب النازل بعاد وثمود وقوم لوط وغيرهم ما كان ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second objection says calamities may test believers, as in the Qur’anic promise to test the steadfast, so suffering alone does not prove its recipients were wrong.
rows.anchor: أن الله تعالى قد ينزل العذاب محنة للمكلفين وابتلاء لهم على ما قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi answers that the stories console Muhammad: God tells him that He inflicted those peoples’ punishment for disbelief, reassuring him that the same account is true.
rows.anchor: أنزل هذه القصص على محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم تسلية وإزالة للحزن عن قلبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An argument against astrological causation says effects cannot arise from a planet alone, a constellation alone, or the planet’s position in one constellation, since those conditions persist or are uniform.
rows.anchor: بأن قال المؤثر في هذه الأشياء ، إما الكواكب أو البروج أو كون الكوكب في البرج المعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Astrologers may answer that a particular alignment with another planet is a necessary condition; without the alignment, the effect does not occur.
rows.anchor: لم لا يجوز أن يكون صدور الأثر عن الكوكب المعين موقوفا على كونه مسامتا مسامتة مخصوصة لكوكب آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That argument excludes effects inherent in planetary natures, but not customary associations God may establish; therefore celestial events do not prove that God created a calamity specifically to warn unbelievers.
rows.anchor: ولكنها لا تدل على أنها ليست مؤثرة بحسب جري العادة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says Moses married the younger daughter and fulfilled the more complete of the two terms.
rows.anchor: روي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال : ( تزوج صغراهما وقضى أوفاهما )

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says Moses fulfilled ten years, then remained with Shuʿayb for another ten.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد قضى الأجل عشر سنين ومكث بعد ذلك عنده عشر سنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conjunction says Moses saw the fire after both completing the term and traveling with his family; it does not show he left as soon as the term ended, contrary to the Qadi.
rows.anchor: يدل على أن ذلك الإيناس حصل عقيب مجموع الأمرين ولا يدل على أنه حصل عقيب أحدهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Traveling with his family does not imply that Moses left alone with his wife; the plural command “stay” confirms a group was present.
rows.anchor: وقوله : { امكثوا } فيه دلالة على الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the phrase about seeing fire was already explained in his commentaries on Ṭā Hā and al-Naml.
rows.anchor: أما قوله : { إنى آنست نارا } فقد مر تفسيره في سورة طه والنمل

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: The Kashshaf author says jadhwa has three dialectal forms, all read, and means a thick piece of wood whether or not fire is on its tip.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) الجذوة باللغات الثلاث وقد قرىء بهن جميعا وهو العود الغليظ

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines jadhwa as a thick fragment of firewood.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج الجذوة القطعة الغليظة من الحطب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier account says night darkened, strong wind scattered the livestock, Moses lost his way, and rain brought severe cold; he wanted a guide or wood to warm the family.
rows.anchor: أظلم عليه الليل في الصحراء وهبت ريح شديدة فرقت ماشيته وضل وأصابهم مطر فوجدوا بردا شديدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The valley bank is its side; the call came from Moses’ right, from the bank and near the tree. “From the tree” is an appositional relation because the tree grew on the bank.
rows.anchor: بدل الاشتمال لأن الشجرة كانت نابتة على الشاطىء كقوله : { لجعلنا لمن يكفر بالرحمان لبيوتهم }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The place is called blessed because Moses’ mission began there and God spoke to him there.
rows.anchor: وإنما وصف البقعة بكونها مباركة لأنه حصل فيها ابتداء الرسالة وتكليم الله تعالى إياه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since migration made believers grieve over leaving home and family, God reminds them that death is inevitable and that dying in His cause earns recompense at their return to Him.
rows.anchor: فقال لهم إن ما تكرهون لا بد من وقوعه فإن كل نفس ذائقة الموت والموت مفرق الأحباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a subtler reading, the self that remains attached to itself must taste death; it should instead attach to God, since every other thing perishes.
rows.anchor: فمن يريد ألا يذوق الموت لا يبقى مع نفسه فإن / النفس ذائقته بل يتعلق بغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attachment to God makes death a return to Him rather than annihilation, as shown by martyrs’ life with God.
rows.anchor: إذا تعلقتم بي فموتكم رجوع إلي وليس بموت

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic saying expresses this reading by saying believers do not die but move from one abode to another.
rows.anchor: وقال عليه السلام : ( المؤمنون لا يموتون بل ينقلون من دار إلى دار )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers’ promised reward contrasts with the Hell surrounding unbelievers and their punishment for their deeds.
rows.anchor: بين ما يكون للمؤمنين وقت الرجوع إليه كما بين من قبل ما يكون للكافرين بقوله : { وإن جهنم لمحيطة بالكافرين }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mention of chambers above believers signals their elevated rank: unlike unbelievers beneath layers of fire, the believers occupy the highest level, with nothing above them.
rows.anchor: فيكونون في أعلى عليين ، فلم يذكر فوقهم شيئا إشارة إلى علو مرتبتهم وارتفاع منزلتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fire beneath the unbelievers hurts when aligned with and touching their feet; water beneath the believers’ chambers is pleasurable regardless of its distance or position.
rows.anchor: فقال في النار من تحت أرجلهم ليحصل الألم بها ، وقال ههنا من تحت الغرف لحصول اللذة به كيف كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command “taste” the punishment would signal the end of a hired worker’s relationship, while “excellent is the wage” comforts believers without suggesting their reward relationship ends.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأن لفظ الأمر يدل على انقطاع التعلق / بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unbelievers’ punishment remains permanently without increase, whereas believers’ reward keeps increasing, as indicated by “the best and more”; unbelievers’ endless duration is established elsewhere.
rows.anchor: الذي يصل إلى الكافر يدوم من غير زيادة والذي يصل إلى المؤمن يزداد على الدوام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience suits present hardship, while reliance suits future needs; the past cannot be recovered or altered.
rows.anchor: ذكر أمرين الصبر والتوكل لأن الزمان ماض وحاضر ومستقبل لكن الماضي لا تدارك له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience and reliance require knowledge of God and of the passing world: knowing worldly things are transient makes patience easier, while knowing God endures supports trust in His provision.
rows.anchor: فمن علم ما سواه علم أنه زائل فيهون عليه الصبر إذ الصبر على الزائل هين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surrounding exhortation suits two groups: those able to leave a place of harm rely on God and migrate, while those unable to leave endure harm and continue worshipping.
rows.anchor: فحصل الناس على قسمين قادر على الخروج وهو متوكل على ربه ، يترك الأوطان ويفارق الأخوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The example of creatures that store nothing for tomorrow shows that God supplies their daily provision and supports reliance upon Him.
rows.anchor: وهو بيان حال الدواب التي لا تدخر شيئا لغد ، ويأتيها كل يوم برزق رغد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi notes four forms of kāʾayyin and says the recited forms are kāʾayyin and kāʾin, with Ibn Kathir associated with the latter reading.
rows.anchor: المسألة الأولى : في كأين لغات أربع ( لا ) غير هذه ( و ) كائن على وزن راع وكأين على وزن ريع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kāʾayyin combines the comparative kāf with ayy, which can function like “who” or “what”; together the form means “how many.”
rows.anchor: كلمة مركبة من كاف التشبيه وأي التي تستعمل استعمال من وما ركبتا وجعل المركب بمعنى كم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is written with nūn to distinguish the compound meaning “how many” from uncombined ka-ayyi, as in the conventional joined spellings of Maʿd Yakrib and Baʿlabakk.
rows.anchor: ولم تكتب إلا بالنون ليفصل بين المركب وغير المركب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kāʾayyin means “how many” and is rarely followed by min, whereas kam often takes min; the particle distinguishes the compound from uncombined ka-ayyi, which cannot take min.
rows.anchor: كأين بمعنى كم لم تستعمل مع من إلا نادرا وكم يستعمل كثيرا من غير من

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: “They do not carry their provision” may mean they are too weak to carry it, that they are tiny creatures such as lice, fleas, or worms, or that they do not store it.
rows.anchor: قيل : لا تحمل لضعفها وقيل هي كالقمل والبرغوث والدود وغيرها وقيل لا تدخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s providing for animals implies by analogy that He provides for humans, so people should trust Him.
rows.anchor: بطريق القياس أي لا شك في أن رزقها ليس إلا بالله فكذلك يرزقكم فتوكلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God provides by creating food plants, by enabling digestion through powers that attract, retain, digest, and expel, and by guiding creatures toward food through smell.
rows.anchor: أما بالنظر إلى الرزق فلأن الله تعالى لو لم يخلق النبات لم يكن للحيوان رزق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some animals do not recognize certain foods until they are put into the mouth; a camel may need yeast or barley fed to it two or three times before recognizing it.
rows.anchor: فإن كثيرا ما يكون البعير لا يعرف الخمير ولا الشعير حتى يلقم مرتين أو ثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saving food does not contradict reliance: a farmer may rely on God while working, whereas someone praying with his heart attached to other people’s possessions does not rely on God.
rows.anchor: بل قد يكون الزارع الحاصد متوكلا والراكع الساجد غير متوكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although human needs are numerous and provision requires work, people have many forms of earning through their hands, feet, sight, speech, understanding, learning, and physical strength.
rows.anchor: فإنه يكتسب بيده كالخياط والنساج وبرجله كالساعي وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has made worldly wealth pass into human ownership even without the owner’s intention: livestock offspring and tree fruit enter property, and inheritance transfers across generations.
rows.anchor: فإن الله ملك الإنسان عمائر الدنيا وجعلها بحيث تدخل في ملكه شاء أم أبى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans are even more deserving of reliance than animals: human provisions and their means are brought within reach, while animals must seek their food or go without.
rows.anchor: فإذن الإنسان لو توكل كان أقرب إلى العقل من توكل الحيوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God hears people’s requests and answers, and knows their unspoken needs and their measure.
rows.anchor: عليم إن سكتم ، لا تخفى عليه حاجتكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who fail to understand have already had their hearts sealed by God.
rows.anchor: من لا يعلم الآن فقد طبع الله على قلبه من قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to be patient consoles Muhammad: the truth of God’s promise means the Prophet’s truthfulness will become clear.
rows.anchor: بقوله : { فاصبر إن وعد الله حق } أي أن صدقك يبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do not let the uncertain unsettle you” requires continued invitation to faith; silence would let unbelievers claim the Prophet has changed his position and lacks firmness.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى وجوب مداومة النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام على الدعاء إلى الإيمان فإنه لو سكت لقال الكافر إنه متقلب الرأي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqman’s wisdom involved gratitude within himself and counsel to others: human excellence consists in becoming complete and helping others become complete.
rows.anchor: وتقديره آتينا لقمان الحكمة حين جعلناه شاكرا في نفسه وحين جعلناه واعظا لغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Be grateful” marks self-perfection, while Luqman’s speech to his son marks completing another; God honors Luqman to illustrate the Prophet’s higher work guiding kin and strangers.
rows.anchor: فقوله : { أن اشكر } إشارة إلى الكمال وقوله : { وإذ قال لقمان لابنه وهو يعظه } إشارة إلى التكميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Teaching one’s child is a familiar duty, whereas enduring the hardship of teaching outsiders is not; this makes the Prophet’s guidance of others especially exemplary.
rows.anchor: فإن إرشاد الولد أمر معاد ، وأما تحمل المشقة في تعليم الأباعد فلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqman begins with the most important counsel, forbidding associationism because it is grave injustice.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا لطيفة وهي أن الله ذكر لقمان وشكر سعيه حيث أرشد ابنه ليعلم منه فضيلة النبي عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shirk wrongs the honored human by directing worship to a base object or by placing worship where it does not belong; it is uniquely grave because no one besides God can be worshipped.
rows.anchor: وأما الإشراك فوضع المعبودية في غير الله تعالى ولا يجوز أن يكون غيره معبودا أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After forbidding shirk and recalling God’s knowledge and power, Luqman commands prayer as sincere worship; prayer existed in earlier religious communities, though its form differed.
rows.anchor: أمره بما يلزمه من التوحيد وهو الصلاة وهي العبادة لوجه الله مخلصا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One who worships God completes himself; enjoining right and forbidding wrong helps complete others, the work of prophets and their learned successors.
rows.anchor: إذا كملت أنت في نفسك بعبادة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order differs from the earlier counsel because Luqman assumed his son already acknowledged God’s existence and therefore first needed prohibition of shirk; commentators report that the son was a polytheist whom Luqman continued to admonish until he accepted Islam.
rows.anchor: ورد في التفسير أن ابنه كان مشركا فوعظه ولم يزل يعظه حتى أسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who enjoin right and forbid wrong will be harmed, so Luqman tells his son to endure what befalls him.
rows.anchor: يعني أن من يأمر بالمعروف وينهى عن المنكر يؤذي فأمره بالصبر عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Among the resolute matters” means obligatory and firmly determined; the verbal noun is used in the sense of its passive object, as in “my eating in the day” for what I eat.
rows.anchor: من الأمور الواجبة المعزومة أي المقطوعة ويكون المصدر بمعنى المفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trust is the burden of moral responsibility, which requires acting against one’s natural disposition; unlike humans, the heavens, earth, and mountains remain as created.
rows.anchor: أي التكليف وهو الأمر بخلاف ما في الطبيعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels do receive commands and prohibitions, but obedience is congenial to their nature, as eating and drinking are to humans; they glorify God without tiring.
rows.anchor: فيسبحون الليل والنهار لا يفترون كما يشتغل الإنسان بأمر موافق لطبعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation calls the trust moral responsibility: the negligent incur liability and the faithful receive honor.
rows.anchor: من قال هو التكليف وسمي أمانة لأن من قصر فيه / فعليه الغرامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation identifies the trust as the declaration that there is no god but God, but al-Razi rejects it because the heavens, earth, and mountains already proclaim divine oneness.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال هو قول لا إله إلا الله وهو بعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations identify the trust with the body’s entrusted organs, or with knowledge of God.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال الأعضاء فالعين أمانة ينبغي أن يحفظها والأذن كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “offering” may be literal presentation, resurrection, or comparison in which the trust is weighed against the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: في العرض وجوه منهم من قال المراد العرض ومنهم من قال الحشر ومنهم من قال المقابلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The heavens and earth” may mean those entities themselves or their inhabitants, with the latter reading supplying an omitted “people of.”
rows.anchor: أن المراد هي بأعيانها ، والثاني : المراد أهلوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The creation’s refusal differs from Iblis’s refusal: prostration was obligatory but the trust was offered, and Iblis acted arrogantly whereas creation humbly feared its incapacity.
rows.anchor: أحدهما : أن هناك السجود كان فرضا ، وههنا الأمانة كانت عرضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trust inspires fear because it resembles a precious, fragile object: one might refuse to accept it for fear of losing it; moral responsibility is both valuable and vulnerable.
rows.anchor: أن يكون عزيزا صعب الحفظ كالأواني من الجواهر التي تكون عزيزة سريعة الانكسار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It also resembles keeping a deposit during a dangerous time: Satan and his forces were attacking those made morally responsible after Adam left the garden.
rows.anchor: والأمر كان كذلك لأن الشيطان وجنوده كانوا في قصد المكلفين إذ الغرض كان بعد خروج آدم من الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It further resembles custody of animals that need food, water, and care; unlike goods safely set in a box, moral responsibility requires continuing cultivation.
rows.anchor: والتكليف كذلك فإنه يحتاج إلى تربية وتنمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One answer says the human accepted the trust from ignorance of its consequences, whereas the heavens and earth knew what it contained; this explains “unjust and ignorant.”
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال تعالى : { إنه كان ظلوما جهولا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second answer says the created things saw their weakness, while the human focused on the trustworthy Lord’s knowledge and power and trusted that He would guard what He entrusted.
rows.anchor: والثاني : أن الأشياء نظرت إلى أنفسهن فرأين ضعفهن فامتنعن ، والإنسان نظر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human’s trust rests on the conviction expressed in “You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”
rows.anchor: وقال : { إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to believing servants to add God-consciousness to faith is evidence that faith remains alongside sin.
rows.anchor: والمراد أن الله تعالى أمر المؤمنين بأن يضموا إلى الإيمان التقوى ، وهذا من أول الدلائل على أن الإيمان يبقى مع المعصية

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The Qadi says believers are commanded to fear God so their faith and its reward are not nullified: avoiding major sins preserves reward, while committing them cancels it.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي : أمرهم بالتقوى ليكلا يحبطوا إيمانهم ، لأن عند الاتقاء من الكبائر يسلم لهم الثواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi answers that exhorting believers to fear God more strongly implies they remain believers even when they fail to do so; grave sin does not remove faith.
rows.anchor: لما أمر المؤمنين بالتقوى دل ذلك على أنه يبقى مؤمنا مع عدم التقوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “in this world” modifies doing good, the verse promises every good-doer a magnificent afterlife reward, namely Paradise, whose perfection reason cannot encompass.
rows.anchor: في الآخرة ، وهي دخول الجنة ، والتنكير في قوله : { حسنة }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the phrase modifies “goodness,” the promise is worldly well-being; some identify it as health, safety, and sufficiency, which the Prophet describes as inexhaustible blessings.
rows.anchor: وأما على التقدير الثاني : فمعناه الذين أحسنوا فلهم في هذه الدنيا حسنة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic saying names security, health, and sufficiency as three blessings without end.
rows.anchor: ثلاثة ليس لها نهاية : الأمن والصحة والكفاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi prefers the afterlife reading: the indefinite “goodness” suggests majesty suited to the lasting afterlife, not transient worldly life.
rows.anchor: أن التنكير في قوله : { حسنة } يدل على النهاية والجلالة والرفعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afterlife reading fits because reward for monotheism and good deeds comes there, while health, security, and sufficiency also reach unbelievers, often more fully.
rows.anchor: حاصلة للكفار ، وأيضا فحصولها للكافر أكثر وأتم من حصولها للمؤمن

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic saying calls worldly life a prison for the believer and a garden for the unbeliever.
rows.anchor: كما قال صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( الدنيا سجن المؤمن وجنة الكافر )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s restrictive force rules out worldly well-being, since worldly blessings are not exclusive to those who do good; it coherently describes afterlife reward.
rows.anchor: يفيد الحصر ، بمعنى أنه يفيد أن حسنة هذه الدنيا لا تحصل إلا للذين أحسنوا ، وهذا باطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation of “God’s earth is vast” says people have no excuse for failing to do good because of their homeland; they should move where worship is possible, as the prophets and righteous did.
rows.anchor: المراد أنه لا عذر ألبتة للمقصرين في الإحسان ، حتى إنهم إن اعتلوا بأوطانهم وبلادهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reading encourages migration from Mecca to Medina and patience in leaving one’s homeland.
rows.anchor: والمقصود منه الترغيب في الهجرة من مكة إلى المدينة والصبر على مفارقة الوطن

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim says “God’s earth” means Paradise: the verse moves from piety to the good reward of eternal residence in the vast Garden.
rows.anchor: قال أبو مسلم : لا يمتنع أن يكون المراد من الأرض أرض الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi prefers the first interpretation of the vast earth, since the following promise of immeasurable reward fits migration and patient endurance.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول عندي أولى ، لأن قوله : { إنما يوفى الصابرون أجرهم بغير حساب } لا يليق إلا بالأول
